column2: Why is more rehabilitation intensity not always better?
column3: Dose must fit tissue healing, cardiovascular reserve, cognition, fatigue and recovery, so exceeding these limits can harm rather than help.

column3: With beta blockade, atrial fibrillation, autonomic dysfunction, pacemakers or chronotropic incompetence, heart rate no longer tracks effort, so perceived exertion and symptoms gain importance.

column2: Why does spasticity management begin with triggers, and why must outcomes be tested in actual tasks?
column3: Pain, infection, constipation, skin injury and poor positioning are addressed first; then, because reducing tone can worsen transfers or standing in someone who relies on it, results are checked in real tasks.

column3: Position upright, remove tight items, search rapidly for bladder blockage and other triggers, monitor blood pressure, and give medication if pressure remains dangerous.

column2: Why should clinicians not estimate quality of life from physical function, and how does this bear on access to rehabilitation?

column2: Why can a previously successful rehabilitation plan fail, and what should lack of progress prompt?
column3: Growth, ageing, pregnancy, new disease and caregiver change can destabilise it; lack of progress prompts review of diagnosis, dose, learning conditions, mood, pain, equipment, environment and the goal itself.
